scenes.title: Activity
scenes.summary: Things are set before the eyes by words that signify things in activity: calling a good man “four-square” is a metaphor without activity, “whose prime is in flower” has it. Homer makes lifeless things alive through metaphor by analogy: the shameless stone, the arrow that flew, the spears longing for flesh, the spear point raging, the waves arched and white-crested; for activity is movement.

scenes.title: Likeness in Things Far Apart
scenes.summary: Metaphors should come from things related but not obvious, as in philosophy it takes a sharp mind to see likeness in things far apart: Archytas' arbitrator and altar, the anchor and the pot-hook, cities “leveled”.

scenes.title: Deception and Surprise
scenes.summary: Most urbane sayings add a deception, so that the hearer learns by the surprise and says to himself, “How true! And I was wrong.” So with apophthegms like Stesichorus' cicadas, with riddles and “novel things”, with jokes made by changing a letter, like Theodorus' jibe at Nicon the citharode, and with verses that end unexpectedly, as “chilblains” for “sandals”.

scenes.title: Words in Two Senses
scenes.summary: Homonymy and metaphor are good when they fit: the empire that was not the beginning of evils, “Anaschetus is not to be endured”, “no more a stranger than you should”, Anaxandrides' “noble to die before doing anything worthy of death”. The briefer and more antithetical, the better, provided the saying is true of its object; the more qualities it has, the more urbane.

scenes.title: Similes, Proverbs and Hyperboles
scenes.summary: Well-liked similes are metaphors made from two terms, like the shield as the cup of Ares and the bow as a stringless lyre; Niceratus as a Philoctetes bitten by Pratys, legs curly as parsley, Philammon sparring with the punching bag. Proverbs are metaphors from species to species, like the Carpathian's hare; hyperboles too are metaphors, adolescent and vehement, like Achilles' refusal, and unfit for an older man.
